posts.quote: DAD CARVED THE FACE, MOM SAVED THE SEEDS, AND THE KIDS GOT THE JOB NOBODY WANTED: SCOOPING OUT THE GUTS.
posts.caption: Every October the newspapers came out and got spread across the kitchen table, and that was how you knew it was pumpkin night. Dad got the big knife and the final say on the face. Mom stood by with a bowl, because not one seed in that house was going to waste. That left the kids, sleeves rolled up past the elbow, reaching into a cold, slimy pumpkin and pulling out handfuls of strings. We complained the whole time. Then the candle went in, the lights went off, and every one of us forgot we ever did.
posts.first:
My little sister refused to touch the inside of a pumpkin, so I did hers and mine every year. Mom roasted the seeds with salt on a cookie sheet and they were gone before they cooled. I can still smell that kitchen.

posts.quote: A QUARTER IN THE JUKEBOX BOUGHT YOU THREE SONGS, AND THE WHOLE DINER HAD TO LISTEN.
posts.caption: Every diner worth its pie had one, glowing in the corner like a church window. You'd lean over the glass and flip through the cards one at a time, reading every title twice. Three songs for a quarter meant real decisions. Pick the wrong one and the whole counter would let you know it. Pick the right one and the cook would start humming along behind the window. It was the only place in town where a kid with a quarter controlled the room.
posts.first:
There was a jukebox at a diner on Route 9 that had the same songs on it for about twelve years. My dad played the same one every single time we stopped. I knew every word by the time I was six.

posts.quote: "DON'T MAKE ME PULL THIS CAR OVER." HE NEVER DID, AND WE NEVER FOUND OUT WHAT HAPPENED IF HE DID.
posts.caption: It always started somewhere around the second hour. Somebody's elbow crossed the invisible line down the middle of the back seat, and somebody else made sure the whole car heard about it. Mom would turn around first, which was a warning. Then Dad's eyes would find you in the rearview mirror, and that was serious. When he finally said the words, the back seat went so quiet you could hear the tires. Nobody knew what happened on the side of the road, and nobody was ever brave enough to find out.
posts.first:
Three of us in the back of a wood-paneled station wagon, no air conditioning, eight hours to Grandma's. Dad said those words at least once per state. He slowed down one time and I thought my brother was going to cry.

posts.character: Humor about today vs. then (the family dog)
posts.quote: We didn't have a garbage disposal. We had a dog under the table and a mother who pretended not to see.
posts.first:
Our beagle Rusty knew exactly which chair the lima beans came from. He'd sit next to me and wait without making a sound. Mom knew the whole time and never said a word.

posts.quote: CLAPPING ERASERS / STAYING AFTER SCHOOL TO BEAT THE CHALK OUT OF THEM WAS SOMEHOW AN HONOR
posts.caption: At the end of the day the teacher would look out over the room and pick two names, and the two of you would try not to look too pleased about it. You'd carry an armload of felt erasers out the back door and bang them together against the brick wall. White clouds of chalk dust went everywhere: your hair, your sweater, your eyebrows. You came home looking like you'd been in a flour fight. Your mother asked what happened. You told her, proud as anything, that you'd been chosen.
posts.first:
Mrs. Albright picked me for erasers about once a week in third grade, and I thought it meant I was her favorite. Years later I figured out she just picked whoever talked the most. There was a white spot on that brick wall the whole time I went there.

posts.quote: EVERY HOLIDAY TABLE HAD A WOBBLY GREEN SALAD WITH SOMETHING FLOATING IN IT THAT NOBODY COULD NAME.
posts.caption: It came out of the refrigerator on Grandma's good glass plate, still shivering from the trip. It was green, it was shaped like a ring, and there was definitely something suspended inside it. Some years it was fruit cocktail. Some years it was shredded carrots. One year there was something that looked like celery and tasted like a mystery. Nobody ever asked for the recipe, and nobody ever dared skip it. It was on the table every Thanksgiving, and somehow it's the dish we miss the most.
posts.first:
My Aunt Ruth made hers with cottage cheese and pineapple, and she was very proud of it. Every one of us took a spoonful to be polite. I'd give anything for one more polite spoonful.

posts.quote: TAIL FINS AS TALL AS A FENCE POST, AND A BACK SEAT BIG ENOUGH TO RAISE A FAMILY IN.
posts.caption: You could spot one from a block away, those chrome fins sweeping up off the back like the car was about to take off. They were longer than some driveways. The back seat was a sofa with doors, and on a long trip you could lay down across it with room to spare. Parking it took a team effort and a prayer. Nobody cared about the gas mileage. When one of those rolled down Main Street on a Saturday night, everybody on the sidewalk turned to watch it go by.
posts.first:
Our neighbor Mr. Hadley had a pink one with fins so sharp my mother made us walk around them. He washed it every Saturday morning and wouldn't let anybody lean on it. When he finally sold it, I think he cried.

posts.quote: THE USHER HAD A FLASHLIGHT AND A LOOK, AND HE KNEW EXACTLY WHICH ROW YOU WERE TALKING IN.
posts.caption: He wore a red jacket with brass buttons and walked the aisle like he owned the place, which as far as we knew, he did. He'd walk you to your seat with that flashlight pointed at the floor, polite as a butler. But start whispering during the picture and that beam would land right on your face. He never said much. He didn't have to. One flash of light and the whole row sat up straight for the rest of the show.
posts.first:
The usher at the Rialto was a tall, skinny fellow named Walt who must have been seventy. He caught my friend Danny with his feet on the seat in front of him and just stood there with the light on his shoes until Danny put them down. We behaved after that.

posts.quote: THE PASSBOOK SAVINGS ACCOUNT / A QUARTER A WEEK, A STAMP IN THE LITTLE BOOK, AND A TELLER WHO MADE YOU FEEL LIKE A MILLIONAIRE
posts.caption: Your first bank account came with a little book that fit in your back pocket, and you guarded it like a passport. Every Saturday you stood on your toes at the counter and slid your quarter across the marble. The teller wrote it in, stamped the date, and handed it back like you were a regular customer. Twice a year the interest showed up, a few cents you didn't do a thing to earn. You'd add it all up on the walk home. It wasn't much, but every penny of it was yours.
posts.first:
I opened mine at the bank downtown with four dollars of birthday money. The teller was a lady with cat-eye glasses who always called me "young man." I was nine and I stood an inch taller every time.

posts.quote: BEFORE YOU PLAYED WITH ONE CHRISTMAS PRESENT, MOM HAD YOU WRITING THANK-YOU NOTES TO EVERY AUNT IN THE STATE.
posts.caption: The paper was barely off the boxes before Mom showed up with a stack of note cards and a pen. You could look at your new things all you wanted. You could not touch them. Dear Aunt Helen, thank you for the socks. Dear Aunt Marge, thank you for the other socks. Every note had to be in your best handwriting and every one had to say something nice and true. It took all morning. And every aunt on the list wrote back to tell your mother what a fine young person you were.
posts.first:
My mother kept a list taped inside the kitchen cabinet of who gave what, so you couldn't get out of a single one. I still write thank-you notes. My hand starts aching at the third one, just like it did then.
